title: Flags, Comparisons and Jumps
summary: Every `if`, loop and `switch` in C++ becomes a **comparison** that sets the flags and a **conditional jump** that reads them. This lesson covers `cmp` and `test`, the family of `j`*cc* jumps and which ones mean signed or unsigned, and the branch-free alternatives `setcc` and `cmov`.
markdown:
## cmp and test

Lesson 7.03 showed that arithmetic sets the flags. Two instructions exist **only** to set them:

| Instruction | Computes | Keeps | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cmp a, b` | a − b | Only the flags; a is unchanged | Comparing two values |
| `test a, b` | a AND b | Only the flags | Checking for zero (`test eax, eax`) or particular bits |

`test eax, eax` is the idiom for "is eax zero?": ANDing a value with itself gives the value, so ZF is set exactly when it is zero, and SF when it is negative.

## Conditional jumps

A conditional jump goes to a label if a condition on the flags holds, and otherwise falls through to the next instruction. The condition names come in signed and unsigned versions, because "less than" means different things for signed and unsigned numbers (lesson 1.02):

| After `cmp a, b`, jump if... | Signed | Unsigned | Flags tested |
|---|---|---|---|
| a == b | `je` / `jz` | `je` / `jz` | ZF = 1 |
| a != b | `jne` / `jnz` | `jne` / `jnz` | ZF = 0 |
| a < b | `jl` | `jb` ("below") | SF ≠ OF / CF = 1 |
| a <= b | `jle` | `jbe` | ZF = 1 or SF ≠ OF / CF = 1 or ZF = 1 |
| a > b | `jg` | `ja` ("above") | ZF = 0 and SF = OF / CF = 0 and ZF = 0 |
| a >= b | `jge` | `jae` | SF = OF / CF = 0 |
| always | `jmp` | `jmp` | none |

So the jump tells you the **type**: `jl`/`jg` after a `cmp` means the compiler treated the values as signed; `jb`/`ja` means unsigned (or pointers, or sizes). When reverse engineering, that is often your first clue to a variable's type.

## An if, compiled

```cpp
int clampHealth(int h)
{
    if (h > 100) h = 100;
    return h;
}
```

```asm
clampHealth PROC
    cmp   ecx, 100        ; compare h with 100
    jle   keep            ; if h <= 100, skip the assignment
    mov   ecx, 100
keep:
    mov   eax, ecx        ; return h
    ret
clampHealth ENDP
```

Notice the **inverted condition**: C++ says "if h > 100, do this", and the compiler writes "if h <= 100, jump over this". That inversion is so common that reading compiled code, you learn to flip conditions automatically.

```demo-asm
title: clampHealth with h = 140
init: ecx=140
    cmp   ecx, 100
    jle   keep
    mov   ecx, 100
keep:
    mov   eax, ecx
    ret
```

With a value of 100 or less in `ecx`, the `jle` would be taken instead and `mov ecx, 100` skipped.

## Branch-free versions: setcc and cmov

A jump that the processor cannot predict is expensive: modern CPUs guess which way each branch goes and start working ahead, and a wrong guess throws that work away (10 to 20 cycles). For simple choices, compilers often avoid the jump entirely:

| Instruction | Effect |
|---|---|
| `setl al` (and `sete`, `setg`, `setb` ...) | al = 1 if the condition holds, else 0: a `bool` result |
| `cmovg eax, edx` (and every other condition) | eax = edx if the condition holds; otherwise eax is unchanged |

```asm
; return a > b;            ; return a > b ? a : b;   (std::max)
cmp   ecx, edx             mov   eax, edx
setg  al                   cmp   ecx, edx
ret                        cmovg eax, ecx
                           ret
```

```demo-asm
title: std::max(8, 3) without a jump
init: ecx=8, edx=3
    mov   eax, edx
    cmp   ecx, edx
    cmovg eax, ecx
    ret
```

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Reading the jump as the C++ condition
> Compilers usually jump *around* the body, so the jump's condition is the opposite of the `if`.

> [!warning] Mixing up `jl` and `jb`
> `jl` is signed less-than, `jb` unsigned. For -1 against 1, `jl` jumps (−1 < 1) and `jb` does not (0xFFFFFFFF is above 1).

> [!warning] Forgetting what set the flags
> A conditional jump uses whatever instruction last set the flags, which is not always the line right above it.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What do `cmp` and `test` compute, and what do they keep?
+ `cmp` subtracts and `test` ANDs their operands; both keep only the flags and throw the result away
- `cmp` compares and stores 1 or 0; `test` checks whether a register is valid
- Both subtract, and both store the result in the first operand
- `cmp` ANDs and `test` subtracts; both keep the result
> That is why a conditional jump comes after them: it reads the flags they set.

? How can you tell from compiled code whether a comparison was signed or unsigned?
- From the `cmp` instruction, which has a signed and an unsigned form
- From the size of the registers used
+ From the jump or set instruction that reads the flags: `l`/`g` are signed, `b`/`a` are unsigned
- You cannot; the information is lost when compiling
> `cmp` is the same either way; the choice of `jl` or `jb` (and so on) shows how the bits were meant.

? What do `setcc` and `cmovcc` do?
- They set and clear the carry flag
- They save the flags to the stack and restore them
- They jump only if a condition holds
+ `setcc` writes 1 or 0 by a condition; `cmovcc` copies only if it holds
> Both avoid a branch, which can be faster when the condition is hard to predict.

? What does `test eax, eax` followed by `jz done` do?
+ Jumps to `done` if eax is zero
- Jumps if eax is not zero
- Compares eax with zero and stores the result
> AND of a value with itself is zero only when the value is zero, setting ZF.

? After `cmp ecx, edx`, the compiler uses `ja`. What does that suggest about ecx and edx?
- They are being compared as signed values
+ They are being compared as unsigned values
- They are floats
> `ja`/`jb` are the unsigned conditions; `jg`/`jl` the signed ones.

? The C++ says `if (x == 0) { ... }`. Which jump is the compiler most likely to emit before the body?
- `je`, to enter the body
- `jmp`, always
+ `jne`, to skip the body
> The jump goes around the body, so its condition is inverted.

? Why do compilers sometimes use `cmov` instead of a jump?
+ To avoid a branch that might be mispredicted
- Because `cmov` is shorter than `mov`
- Because jumps cannot be conditional
> A mispredicted branch costs many cycles; a conditional move never mispredicts.
```
ideas:
- Work through the `clampHealth` demonstration on paper with `ecx` = 50: which flags does `cmp` set, and which line runs after `jle`?

- In a disassembled function from your own code, find every conditional jump and write next to it the C++ condition it implements (remember to invert).
